newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Klima says reluctant 'yes' to top job.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Klima says reluctant 'yes' to top job.

text.p: Austria's chancellor-designate Viktor Klima reluctantly accepted the job at the helm of goverment after Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's exit from politics but said the move did not quite fit in with his plans.

A tightlipped Klima, having shunned the public spotlight for days, offered only one sentence to comment on his meteoric rise through the ranks of Austrian politics to government head in less than five years.
"I did have a different plan for my life, but I guess I'm going to do it," he told Austrian state television late on Saturday over a mobile telephone.

The line then broke up and there was no further word from Klima. Nobody answered the phones at his office in the Finance Ministry and callers to his listed Vienna home telephone number were kindly asked to leave a message on the answering machine.
"It's like he disappeared into a black hole. I have no idea where he is right now," a senior source inside Klima's Social Democratic Party told Reuters.
Klima said earlier he had been called in by Vranitzky for an early morning chat and told him he was happy to remain finance minister.
"I am finance minister and I like my job. I have made it clear to Vranitzky that I want to be a part of his team until the end of 1998," he said.
But Vranitzky, 59, speaking to reporters after announcing his resignation and withdrawal from political life, said he had finally managed to twist Klima's arm.
"He said he had no intention to take this job, but I convinced him that my plans were better in the medium to long term," he said.
Klima, 49, entered politics in 1992 after a long spell at oil and energy group OMV. After three years at the Transport Ministry, he became finance minister in January 1996.
The telegenic politician repeatedly claimed he wanted to return to industry once his political career was over, telling journalists he would like to set up his own business.
He scored his biggest victory in politics when he pushed through the sale of flagship bank Creditanstalt, a conservative stronghold, to Social Democrat-controlled Bank Austria last weekend.

Conservative anger at the prospect of losing control over "their" bank had threatened to break up the uneasy government coalition of dominant Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party. The survival of the partnership was almost unilaterally credited to Klima's savvy political manoeuvering.

The two parties have ruled Austria together for the past 10 years, but had to renew their coalition after a snap general election in October 1995 forced by the People's Party over a deadlocked budget dispute.
Klima left it to Vranitzky to announce the sale of Creditanstalt after 11 hours of crisis talks among coalition leaders last Sunday.
But analysts said he had proved that he could live up to his title as crown prince and heir-apparent in Vienna's political hierarchy.
Voter surveys show that Klima, a chain smoker, has a high profile with Austria's electorate and ranks ahead of Vranitzky as one of its most popular politicians.

But he reportedly promised his second wife, whom he married two years ago, and his two grown children that he would leave the political arena by the year 2000, one year after the next scheduled general elections.
